Stated Claim / Post Context:
Jurors shown distressing photos of the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies stuffed inside surfboard bags - after top cop broke down on the stand during Beau Lamarre-Condon's murder trial

Follow Daily Mail's live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon's murder trial.

Actual Article Body:
By CHARLOTTE KARP, SENIOR NEWS REPORTER

Updated:  16:41 AEST, 7 October 2026

Jurors were shown distressing images of the surfboard bags containing the bodies of Jesse Baird and his boyfriend Luke Davies in court on Wednesday.

Accused killer Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly tried to hide the body bags at a rural property in Bungonia under rocks, tree branches and foliage, but photos showed the blue bags were clearly visible underneath.

Lamarre-Condon allegedly stacked one body on top of the other.

Now-retired senior sergeant Greg Moon told the court both bodies were contained within two surfboard bags - an inner bag and an outer bag.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of domestic violence-related murder over the alleged shooting murders of Jesse Baird, 26, and Davies, 29 on February 19, 2024.

He has also pleaded not guilty to one count of aggravated break and enter after he allegedly broke into Baird's Paddington home and stole his phone and wallet in August 2023.

Follow Daily Mail's live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon's murder trial below.

Jesse Baird's body was allegedly shoved inside three bags - a black garbage bag and two surfboard bags, the court heard.

Jurors were shown distressing images of the surfboard bags containing the bodies of Baird and his boyfriend Luke Davies.

Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly tried to hide the body bags at a rural property in Bungonia under rocks, tree branches and foliage, but photos showed the blue bags were clearly visible underneath.

Lamarre-Condon allegedly stacked one body on top of the other.

Now-retired senior sergeant Greg Moon told the court both bodies were contained within two surfboard bags - an inner bag and an outer bag.

Investigators removed the outer bags and sent them off for forensic testing.

Mr Moon said the outer bags contained 'a number of maggots and insects, along with decompositional fluids'.

Jurors were shown a photo of one of the inner bags. The bag was closed, but insects were clearly visible on the outside.

Another photo showed the inner bag containing Baird's body.

More than half his torso was covered with a black garbage bag, while the rest was inside the inner surfboard bag.

Mr Moon will continue his evidence at 10am on Thursday.

Jesse Baird and Luke Davies' (pictured) bodies were so badly decomposed that cops identified them by comparing their jewellery to their photos on Instagram.

Senior Sergeant Christine Abela told the court after lunch on Wednesday that Baird's family were at the scene in Bungonia when the bodies were found.

Ms Abela told the court there were black garbage bags near the bodies.

Inside the garbage bags were two keys - one key was to an iron security door, and another house key that opened the front door of Baird's rental property.

A senior cop has broken down on the stand while describing the moment she realised the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies (pictured) were nearby.

Senior Sergeant Christine Abela (pictured below, far left) told the court police were searching for the bodies at a property in Bungonia, about 200km south of Sydney.

The search effort lasted a few days, until they arrived at a fence line near a Greek monastery.

'As soon as I got out of the car, there was a strong smell,' she said.

Ms Abela told the court through tears that she recognised it as the smell of a decomposing body.

The smell was stronger as she approached the fence.

She then saw two silver and blue surfboard bags stacked on top of each other, covered with branches and stones.

Justice Natalie Adams decided to adjourne the court slightly earlier for lunch.

The matter will resume at 2pm.

Beau Lamarre-Condon (pictured) allegedly drove the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies to Bungonia with a female friend, who bought him an angle grinder from Bunnings on the way.

Senior Sergeant Christine Abela told the court that Lamarre-Condon's friend, known by the pseudonym Elizabeth Kennedy for legal reasons, walked in
